records.subject: hemophilia_a
records.claim: Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of coagulation factor VIII.

grounded.byte_quote: Hemophilia A and B result from factor VIII and factor IX protein deficiency or dysfunction, respectively, and are characterized by prolonged and excessive bleeding after minor trauma or sometimes even spontaneously.
discards: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1404/ (GeneReviews Hemophilia A) — authoritative and would also support the fact, but not fetched/quoted; redundant once StatPearls provided a direct verbatim quote.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560494/ (Acquired Hemophilia, StatPearls) — discarded: covers autoantibody-mediated acquired factor VIII deficiency, a different etiology than the congenital factor-deficiency relation asserted by the fact.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560792/ (Hemophilia B) and NBK580494 (Factor V Deficiency) — discarded: about factor IX / factor V, not the hemophilia_a → factor_viii edge.
grounded.note: ENTAILED. The fetched StatPearls "Hemophilia" page states "Hemophilia A and B result from factor VIII and factor IX protein deficiency or dysfunction, respectively." The distributive "respectively" pairs the first subject (Hemophilia A) with the first object (factor VIII), so the source directly asserts Hemophilia A → factor VIII deficiency. Direction is correct (subject hemophilia_a maps to object factor_viii); no inferential leap required. The "or dysfunction" clause broadens beyond pure deficiency but the deficiency relation the fact asserts is explicitly present.

verify.refute_attempt: Strongest refutation: the quote uses a "respectively" coordination — "Hemophilia A and B result from factor VIII and factor IX protein deficiency or dysfunction, respectively." One must rely on the "respectively" binding to map Hemophilia A to factor VIII (and B to IX) rather than the reverse; the sentence does not name "Hemophilia A is caused by factor VIII" in an uncoordinated, standalone form. Additionally the quote says "deficiency or dysfunction," whereas the FACT asserts only "deficiency." However, the refutation fails: "respectively" unambiguously binds A→VIII per standard English distributive reading, and "deficiency" is explicitly one of the listed mechanisms, so the causal edge (Hemophilia A caused by factor VIII deficiency) is directly stated, not inferred.

records.subject: hemophilia_a
records.claim: Hemophilia A is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.

grounded.byte_quote: An X-linked, recessive hemorrhagic trait or gene induces Hemophilia A.
discards: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551607/ (Hemophilia, StatPearls) — general hemophilia overview, not the dedicated Hemophilia A entry; discarded in favor of the disease-specific page.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1404/ (Hemophilia A, GeneReviews) — also authoritative/primary, but I fetched the StatPearls entry which yielded a single verbatim sentence naming both 'X-linked' and 'recessive' for Hemophilia A; not needed as second source.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557383/ (Genetics, X-Linked Inheritance) — describes the inheritance mode generically, does not assert the specific hemophilia_a edge.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7704156/ and PMC9600608 — narrow papers on skewed X-inactivation in carrier females; tangential to the base inheritance-pattern claim.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16684001/ — abstract on genetic diagnosis of bleeding disorders; not a definitional inheritance-pattern statement.
grounded.note: ENTAILED. The fetched StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf, NIH) Hemophilia A page states verbatim in its Etiology section: "An X-linked, recessive hemorrhagic trait or gene induces Hemophilia A." This directly names the subject (Hemophilia A) and asserts both qualifiers of the object (X-linked, recessive) as the inheritance/causal trait, forcing the edge hemophilia_a -> x_linked_recessive. Direction is correct: the source attributes the X-linked-recessive trait TO Hemophilia A (the disease is the subject), not the reverse. No interpretive leap required.

verify.refute_attempt: Strongest refutation: argue the quote states only that an "X-linked, recessive ... trait or gene induces Hemophilia A" — describing the causative gene/trait, not explicitly asserting the disease's inheritance pattern. This fails: (1) describing the disease-causing gene as X-linked recessive IS the standard way of stating the inheritance pattern in clinical genetics; (2) the immediately following sentence reinforces "Hemophilia A's X-linked trait..."; (3) the page separately gives the textbook X-linked recessive transmission rules — carrier females transmit to 50% of sons, affected males pass carrier status to all daughters and to no sons. The edge (Hemophilia A = X-linked recessive) is directly stated and corroborated, so the refutation does not hold.

records.subject: hemophilia_a
records.claim: Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the aPTT with a normal PT.

grounded.byte_quote: Hemophiliacs have an elevated aPTT and a normal PT/INR, as well as normal bleeding time and platelet count.
discards: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK604215/ (Interpretation of Blood Clotting Studies, StatPearls): only states PTT can 'identify' factor VIII deficiency / hemophilia A — names the intrinsic-pathway association but does NOT assert prolonged aPTT with normal PT, so it gives direction at best, not full entailment.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507772/ (Partial Thromboplastin Time, StatPearls): states 'Factor VIII deficiency characterizes Hemophilia A... This produces an intrinsic coagulation pathway defect and thus elevated PTT' — entails hemophilia_a -> elevated aPTT but is silent on PT being normal, so it grounds only half the relation. Strong secondary corroborator, not chosen as primary because it omits the normal-PT clause.
https://cdho.org/factsheets/hemophilia-a/ (CDHO factsheet): dental-hygiene regulatory body, secondary/non-authoritative for coagulation lab patterns — discarded.
https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/779322-workup (Medscape): secondary clinical reference, not a primary/NIH source — not fetched/used.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK580494/ (Factor V Deficiency): wrong factor (V, not VIII) — irrelevant to this edge.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10919413/ (Factor VIII inhibitors): about acquired inhibitors/assay diagnosis, not the baseline congenital hemophilia A aPTT/PT pattern — off-target.
grounded.note: ENTAILED. The chosen quote from NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls 'Bleeding Disorders' (NBK541050) states both halves of the fact in a single sentence: hemophiliacs (factor VIII deficiency = hemophilia A) have 'an elevated aPTT and a normal PT/INR'. Elevated/prolonged aPTT + normal PT = the exact hemophilia_a -> aptt relation asserted, with no inferential leap. The subject (hemophilia) and predicate (aPTT prolonged, PT normal) match directly; direction (deficiency -> test prolongation) is correct. The only minor generalization is that 'hemophiliacs' covers both A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX); the identification of hemophilia A with factor VIII deficiency is independently confirmed verbatim on NBK507772 ('Factor VIII deficiency characterizes Hemophilia A... thus elevated PTT'), so the factor-VIII-specific attribution is also grounded, not assumed.

verify.refute_attempt: Tried to refute on two fronts. (1) The quoted sentence says "Hemophiliacs" generically, and the page (StatPearls "Bleeding Disorders") covers Hemophilia A, Hemophilia B, and von Willebrand disease — so "elevated aPTT, normal PT/INR" might not specifically attach to Factor VIII deficiency. This fails: a second sentence on the same page states "The aPTT, a measure of the intrinsic pathway, is elevated due to low FVIII levels," explicitly tying the elevated aPTT to low Factor VIII (Hemophilia A). (2) "elevated aPTT" vs the FACT's "prolongs the aPTT" — these are equivalent (prolonged clotting time = elevated aPTT value), so no semantic gap. Both refutation attempts fail; the edge (Factor VIII deficiency -> prolonged/elevated aPTT with normal PT) is directly stated.

discards: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32809627/ — PubMed abstract/citation stub for the same StatPearls chapter; discarded in favor of the full primary text on NCBI Bookshelf.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541050/ — 'Bleeding Disorders' StatPearls covers hemophilia broadly, not specific to the hemophilia B → factor IX relation; less direct.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gtr/conditions/C0008533/ — Genetic Testing Registry registry entry, not a narrative authoritative text with a quotable causal sentence.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8484143/ — murine bone-mass model paper; supports factor IX/Christmas disease link but is a specialized research article, not the primary clinical reference.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8627312/ — clinical genetics review; corroborates but secondary to the chosen StatPearls chapter.
clinicaltrials.gov PDFs (NCT03861273, NCT01425723, NCT02695160) — trial protocols, not authoritative descriptive references for disease etiology.
grounded.note: ENTAILED. The fetched StatPearls page states verbatim that 'Hemophilia B, also known as Christmas disease' results from 'inadequate production of factor IX' (a defect in the F9 gene). This directly equates the alias Christmas disease with hemophilia B and names factor IX deficiency as the cause, so the relation hemophilia_b → factor_ix is forced by the quote with no inference required. The source frames it as a defect in F9 causing inadequate factor IX production, which is the molecular basis of the factor IX deficiency; this is the standard equivalence (deficiency = inadequate production), not a leap.

verify.refute_attempt: Strongest refutation: the quote attributes the root cause to an F9 gene defect, with factor IX deficiency as the downstream mechanism — arguably "caused by a gene defect," not "caused by a deficiency." This fails: the quote explicitly states the F9 defect leads to "inadequate production of factor IX" (= factor IX deficiency) and names the disease as Hemophilia B (Christmas disease). The gene-defect framing entails, rather than contradicts, the FACT. The relation Hemophilia B/Christmas disease <-> inadequate production of factor IX is stated directly and verbatim.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551607/ (StatPearls Hemophilia, general) — covers both A and B; less specific to the hemophilia_b subject than NBK560792, so not used as the primary anchor.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557383/ (StatPearls Genetics, X-Linked Inheritance) — explains X-linked recessive mechanism generally but does not tie it specifically to hemophilia B as the named subject.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541050/ (StatPearls Bleeding Disorders) — broader bleeding-disorder overview, not the disease-specific subject node.
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/349662530_Hemophilia_B (ResearchGate PDF) — secondary/aggregator host; primary NCBI source preferred and obtained.
grounded.note: ENTAILED. The fetched StatPearls page states verbatim: "Hemophilia B primarily follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance." This names the subject (Hemophilia B) and the predicate/object (X-linked recessive inheritance) with correct direction (hemophilia_b → x_linked_recessive). No inferential leap is required; the source asserts the exact relation. A corroborating sentence on the same page ("Hemophilia A and B are both inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern...") reinforces it. The qualifier "primarily" reflects that some cases arise from de novo/spontaneous mutation, but the inheritance MODE when inherited is X-linked recessive, which matches the fact.

verify.refute_attempt: Tried to undercut the edge on two angles. (1) The byte_quote hedges with "primarily follows," and the page adds that the defect "can occur either through X-linked inheritance or a spontaneous de novo mutation" — arguably weakening "is inherited X-linked recessive." But a de novo mutation is the absence of inheritance, not a competing inheritance pattern, so it does not contradict the stated inheritance mode. (2) "Carrier females may also experience occasional bleeding symptoms" — this concerns phenotype expression in carriers, not the inheritance pattern, and is fully consistent with X-linked recessive inheritance. Refutation fails: a second, unhedged sentence on the same page states "Hemophilia A and B are both inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern," directly and redundantly asserting the edge.

discards: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK459222/ — duplicate/legacy /sites/ path of the same StatPearls article; redundant with the canonical /books/ URL actually fetched.

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083708/ — PubMed citation stub for the same StatPearls article; the full Bookshelf page is the better primary source and was fetched directly.
grounded.note: ENTAILED. The fetched quote states the disease is "caused by the qualitative or quantitative deficiency of the pro-von Willebrand factor," which directly asserts von_willebrand_disease → deficiency of von_willebrand_factor with the exact subject→object direction of the FACT. A corroborating Introduction sentence ("Any qualitative or quantitative deficiency of pro-von Willebrand factor will lead to an increased bleeding tendency, and this syndrome is called Von Willebrand disease") states the same relation. verify.refute_attempt: Strongest refutation: (1) the source says "pro-von Willebrand factor" (the precursor protein), not "von Willebrand factor" as the FACT states; (2) the source pairs "qualitative OR quantitative deficiency," meaning some VWD (qualitative/type 2) involves dysfunctional factor present in normal amounts rather than a true deficiency, so reducing the cause to "a deficiency" is incomplete. However, neither defeats the relation: "quantitative deficiency" is explicitly a deficiency, pro-VWF is the VWF precursor, and the source's verbatim "caused by ... deficiency" directly asserts the deficiency-causes-disease edge.
